title: Managing a stage boundary: the release planning workshop
blurb: Explain what managing a stage boundary gives the board in an agile project, and the purpose and topics of the release planning workshop.
question: Near the end of a stage, teams review the project canvas, backlog and release map, set team OKRs and break key activities into user stories. Which workshop is this, and which process does it support?

teach.h: Getting the board ready to decide
teach.body: Managing a stage boundary lets the project manager give the board enough information to review the success of the current stage, review the updated release map, approve the next stage plan (itself an updated release map) and confirm that the business justification and the risks are still acceptable. The board then decides in directing a project.

teach.h: From stage end to next stage

steps.label:
Project
dashboard
steps.sub: stage end status for the board

teach.caption: The last step happens in directing a project.

teach.body: In 'prepare the next stage plan', the PM and project team review and, if needed, update the PID components, decide which lessons to apply to the next stage and add the next stage's detail to the release map. The project dashboard takes the place of the end stage report. If a stage is forecast to exceed tolerance, the same process is used to prepare an exception plan for the board.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.15, Table 13.4; PRINCE2 7 manual ch 18

items.label: First stage boundary; release planning workshop for initiation
Stage boundary; release planning for subsequent stages
No boundary at its end: closing a project instead

teach.caption: A stage boundary can also be used at any time to prepare an exception plan.

teach.body: There are two versions: one held during initiation and one for subsequent stages. The PM defines the participants, sets dates and invites everyone. Its purpose is a shared understanding of the project's objectives, teams aligned with the vision and a jointly planned next stage. Participants review the project canvas, project backlog and release map, define measurable team OKRs, break key activities into user stories and update the release map.

steps.label: Introduction
steps.sub: present canvas, project backlog, release map; feedback

steps.label: Release planning
steps.sub: user stories; update the release map

teach.body: Objectives and key results come from John Doerr's goal-setting framework. The objective is a clear, aspirational goal; the key results are specific, measurable outcomes that show progress towards it. Team OKRs set at the stage boundary guide the next stage and measure its success.

Oakmere College's student enrolment app reaches the end of stage 2. Project manager Nadia Hussain invites the two teams and CPO Ben Walsh to a release planning workshop. They review the canvas, project backlog and release map, set the objective 'Make enrolment effortless' with the key result 'average enrolment under ten minutes', and turn priority features into user stories. Nadia updates the release map and project dashboard so executive Carol Fenwick's board can approve stage 3.

teach.text: Release planning (stage boundary) updates the RELEASE MAP and team OKRs for the next stage; team planning (managing product delivery) produces the TEAM PLAN for the next iteration. And there is no stage boundary at the end of the final stage: closing a project takes its place.

items: Stage boundary: board reviews the stage and updated release map, approves the next stage plan, confirms justification and risks.
Next stage plan = updated release map; project dashboard replaces the end stage report.
Prepare the next stage plan: update PID parts, apply lessons, detail the release map.
Release planning workshop: during initiation and for subsequent stages.
Topics: introduction, OKR definition, release planning, wrap-up.
OKR: aspirational objective plus measurable key results.

summary: You can now explain what managing a stage boundary gives the board in an agile project and the purpose and topics of the release planning workshop. You can also tell release planning from team planning.

A.q: Which is a purpose of the 'managing a stage boundary' process?
options: To assign work and keep the stage within tolerance
To control the link between the PM and the team
To confirm acceptance of the project product
To help the board confirm continued justification
A.why: A stage boundary gives the board the information to confirm continued business justification and acceptability of the risks, among other things (13.7.1).

A.q: Which topic of the release planning workshop defines or updates team OKRs?
A.why: OKR definition sets a clear set of OKRs to guide progress and measure success (Table 13.16).

whyNot.1: Release planning turns key activities into user stories and updates the release map.
whyNot.2: The introduction presents the canvas, project backlog and release map for feedback.

A.q: Which stage boundary activity reviews and updates the PID components, applies lessons and updates the release map for the next stage?
A.why: Prepare the next stage plan covers these steps (Table 13.15).

whyNot.0: Report highlights is a controlling a stage activity that updates the project dashboard.
whyNot.1: Evaluate stage status reviews progress during the stage, in a progress review.
whyNot.3: Requesting project authorization ends initiation, asking the board to approve the PID.

B.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, what serves as the next stage plan that the board approves?
B.why: The board approves the next stage plan as an updated release map (13.7.1).

whyNot.0: Team plans cover an iteration and are produced by delivery teams.
whyNot.2: The project backlog holds the epics; it is not a plan.
whyNot.3: The project canvas is the business case.

B.q: Which topic of the release planning workshop breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map?
B.why: The release planning topic breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map (Table 13.16).

whyNot.0: OKR definition sets the team OKRs.
whyNot.1: The introduction reviews existing artifacts and gathers feedback.
whyNot.3: Wrap-up reviews the outputs at the end.

B.q: In the introduction topic of the release planning workshop, what is presented for feedback?
options: Project canvas, project backlog and release map
Team dashboards and the current team plans
Personas and the project Definition of Ready
Agilometer results and agile risk plans
B.why: The introduction presents the project canvas, project backlog, release map and other useful documents (Table 13.16).

whyNot.1: Team dashboards and plans belong to team-level work.
whyNot.2: Personas and the project DoR are project initiation workshop topics.
whyNot.3: Agilometer results are reviewed in the agile enablement workshop.

C.q: Which process prepares the updated release map for the next stage, and which directing activity approves it?
options: Controlling a stage; authorize a stage or exception plan
Managing product delivery; authorize the project
Managing a stage boundary; authorize a stage or exception plan
C.why: The stage boundary prepares the updated release map (13.7.1) and the board approves it in 'authorize a stage or exception plan' (Table 13.4).

whyNot.0: The board activity is right, but the next stage plan is prepared at the stage boundary, not in controlling a stage.
whyNot.1: Authorize initiation approves the brief and the release map for initiation.
whyNot.2: Managing product delivery is team work; authorize the project approves the PID.

C.q:
Which two statements about managing a stage boundary are correct?
1. The release planning workshop held during initiation plans the next stage.
2. Iteration planning is a release planning workshop topic.
3. Team OKRs are defined or updated in the release planning workshop.
4. A stage boundary is held at the end of the final stage to plan closure.
C.why: The release planning workshop during initiation plans the next stage (13.7.4.1), and its OKR definition topic sets team OKRs (Table 13.16).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: iteration planning is a team planning topic.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: iteration planning is team planning, and the final stage ends with closing a project.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the final stage ends with closing a project, not a boundary.

C.q: A team agrees 'Average repair booking takes under two minutes' to show progress towards 'Make reporting a repair effortless'. What is the first statement, and where is it set?
options: A key result; project canvas workshop
A key result; release planning workshop
C.why: A specific, measurable outcome is a key result, and team OKRs are defined in the release planning workshop (12.3.2.3, Table 13.16).

whyNot.0: It is measurable, so it is a key result; team planning does not set OKRs.
whyNot.1: It is a key result, but OKRs are not a canvas workshop topic.
whyNot.3: The workshop is right, but the aspirational goal is the objective; this is the key result.

reteach.title: Planning the next leg of a long walk
reteach.question: How does a group walking a long-distance trail handle each overnight stop?

blocks.h: At each hostel, look back and plan the next leg
blocks.body: Each evening the group looks at the whole route map, agrees a goal for tomorrow ('reach the coast') with measurable markers ('over the ridge by noon'), and redraws the next leg on the map. The trip organizer then decides whether to carry on. Tomorrow morning, each small group plans its own pace: that is team planning, not release planning.

blocks.text: The evening plan is the next leg (stage); each morning's pace plan is the iteration's team plan.

explain.body: The stage boundary equips the board to review the stage, review the updated release map, approve the next stage plan and confirm justification and risks.

test.q: Managing a stage boundary gives the board the information it needs to do which of these?
test.why: Approving the next stage plan (an updated release map) is one of the four purpose points (13.7.1).

whyNot.1: Iteration plans are team plans produced in managing product delivery.
whyNot.2: The project brief is approved in authorize initiation, before initiation.
whyNot.3: The PM authorizes work packages in controlling a stage.

explain.body: The first stage boundary comes towards the end of the initiation stage. It repeats at the end of every later stage except the final one, which ends with closing a project.

test.q: When is managing a stage boundary first used?
options: At the end of the final stage
At the start of each iteration
Towards the end of the initiation stage
test.why: The first stage boundary prepares the next stage near the end of initiation (13.7.4.1; PRINCE2 7 process model).

whyNot.0: The final stage ends with closing a project.
whyNot.1: Nothing precedes starting up; the mandate triggers it.
whyNot.2: Iterations are planned in team planning, not at a stage boundary.

explain.body: For the release planning workshop, the PM defines who takes part, sets the dates and invites the participants, just as for the workshops in starting up and initiating.

test.q: Who defines the participants for the release planning workshop, sets the dates and invites them?
test.why: In managing a stage boundary, the PM defines participants, sets dates and invites them (13.7.3).

whyNot.0: The executive chairs the board that later approves the next stage.
whyNot.2: The CPO takes part and prioritizes, but does not organize the workshop.
whyNot.3: The team coach facilitates team-level workshops.

explain.body: An OKR pairs a clear, aspirational objective with specific, measurable key results that show progress towards it.

test.q: In an OKR, what is the objective?
options: A user story with acceptance criteria
A tolerance set by the board
test.why: The objective is a clear, aspirational goal; key results are specific, measurable outcomes (12.3.2.3).

whyNot.0: A measurable outcome is a key result.
whyNot.1: User stories describe requirements, not objectives.
whyNot.3: Tolerances limit deviation; they are not OKRs.
